questions.prompt: Two different keys have the same hash. What must a correct lookup do?
options: Treat the two keys as one key
Increase every hash value by one
Compare the actual keys of the candidates
Return the first entry in the bucket
questions.explanation: Equal hashes do not prove equal keys. The first entry may simply be a collision.

questions.prompt: How do chaining and open addressing differ?
options: Both always require a directory of size 2^g
Chaining forbids duplicate keys, whereas open addressing allows them
Open addressing always uses overflow pages on disk
Chaining links entries together; open addressing probes slots in the table
questions.explanation: Chaining stores a linked chain, while open addressing searches for another slot. A directory belongs to extendible hashing and is not a general requirement.

questions.prompt: A table has 4 slots and uses linear probing. h(9)=1; slots 1 and 2 are full, and slot 3 is empty. Where is the new entry inserted?
options: Slot 3
Slot 1, overwriting its entry
Slot 0, regardless of its state
The insertion must be rejected
questions.explanation: Linear probing advances through 1 and 2 to 3. It does not overwrite an existing entry.

questions.prompt: What can happen if 20 keys enter the same chain?
options: A lookup needs only one key comparison because hashing is already complete
A lookup may need to check many entries
Only insertion slows down; every lookup still reads one entry
A long chain proves that every key in it is a duplicate
questions.explanation: A long chain increases the work required. Constant-time hash computation does not make the entire lookup constant-time.

questions.prompt: What does an associative array map?
options: Each value to exactly one key, even when values repeat
The position of a key in sorted order to its rank
Keys to values
Each hash value to exactly one key, forbidding collisions
questions.explanation: A hash table implements a key→value mapping. It does not inherently provide key order as a search tree does.

questions.prompt: Which predicate is best suited to a hash index on code?
options: code BETWEEN 10 AND 90
code > 42
ORDER BY code
code = 42
questions.explanation: Equality identifies a bucket directly. Hashing does not preserve ranges or order.

questions.prompt: Why can hashing support GROUP BY?
options: Tuples with the same group key enter the same partition
Every partition always contains only one key
Hashing automatically sorts tuples in ascending order
Hashing eliminates the need for state in every aggregate
questions.explanation: Equal keys always enter the same partition, although different keys can still collide.

questions.prompt: With h(k)=k mod 8, what can be concluded about keys 6 and 14?
options: 14 always follows 6 in every scan
They enter the same bucket but remain different keys
They are the same key because their hashes match
They enter two consecutive buckets
questions.explanation: Both 6 mod 8 and 14 mod 8 equal 6. A hash value proves neither key equality nor ordering.

questions.prompt: To remove duplicates on (A,B), what is the most direct hashing strategy?
options: Hash only A, then treat every key in a bucket as a duplicate
Hash B, but compare only A when removing duplicates
Hash the pair (A,B), then compare the complete pair
Hash the entire tuple, including columns outside DISTINCT(A,B)
questions.explanation: Hashing the complete grouping key consistently brings duplicates together. An entry address or input position does not establish equality.

questions.prompt: A join performs many equality checks. How can a hash index help?
options: Eliminate the need to check collisions
Guarantee output sorted by the join key
Turn every inequality into equality
Find inner candidates using the join key
questions.explanation: Hash lookups narrow the candidate search, but key comparisons remain necessary and the output is not sorted.

questions.prompt: What makes up a bucket in static chained hashing?
options: A primary page and its associated overflow pages
Only one tuple
The entire directory and all data pages
A complete B+ tree in every case
questions.explanation: A bucket consists of its primary page and overflow chain. It need not occupy just one page.

questions.prompt: There are N=7 primary buckets and h(k)=k mod 7. In which bucket does the search for key 23 begin?
questions.explanation: 23=3 × 7+2. Buckets are numbered 0..6; the original key is not used directly as the bucket number.

questions.prompt: In the slide cost model, how many I/Os does a lookup need if no overflow is involved and the page is not cached?
options: Always 2
N
questions.explanation: Only the primary bucket page is read. A cost of 0 would require a caching assumption that was not given.

questions.prompt: An insertion changes one primary page without overflow, and the page is initially uncached. What is its read-plus-write I/O cost?
options: Always 4
questions.explanation: One read and one write are required. Counting only the read omits the write of the modified page.

questions.prompt: A searched-for key may be on the second overflow page after the primary page. How many page reads are needed to follow this entire path?
questions.explanation: Reading the primary page and then two overflow pages requires 3 reads. The primary page is part of the access path.

questions.prompt: A bucket contains 10 entries. Each page holds at most 3 entries, and all pages except the last are full. How many overflow pages are needed in addition to the primary page?
questions.explanation: The bucket needs ceil(10/3)=4 pages in total, so 3 are overflow pages. Answering 4 forgets that the primary page is already included.

questions.prompt: An unsuccessful lookup must search an uncached bucket with one primary page and 3 overflow pages. How many pages must it read before concluding that the key is absent?
questions.explanation: An unsuccessful search checks the entire chain: 1 primary+3 overflow=4 reads. Stopping at the primary page could miss a later entry.

questions.prompt: In a workload, 80% of lookups read 1 page and 20% read 4 pages in an overflow chain. What is the expected number of page reads per lookup?
questions.explanation: The weighted mean is 0.8 × 1+0.2 × 4=1.6. The value 2.5 averages the two cases without accounting for their frequencies.

questions.prompt: A primary bucket contains keys 4 and 12 with the same h(k). Does that mean the keys are duplicates?
options: No; sharing a bucket only establishes a hash collision
Yes; a bucket may contain only one search key
Yes; keys on the same page are always equal
No; hash functions never produce collisions
questions.explanation: 4 and 12 are different even if their hashes match. Bucket membership does not establish search-key equality.

questions.prompt: Two hash indexes have the same average bucket occupancy. Index A has a few very long chains, while B is fairly balanced. What does the average conceal?
options: A guarantee that A and B have the same maximum lookup cost
Tail latency and uneven lookup costs
The fact that A must have fewer data entries than B
The fact that B never needs key comparisons
questions.explanation: Hot or long chains make some lookups much more expensive. Average occupancy does not determine the maximum or distribution of lookup costs.

questions.prompt: How many directory entries are there when global depth g=4?
questions.explanation: The directory has 2^g=16 entries, rather than g entries.

questions.prompt: With g=4 and a bucket of local depth d=2, how many directory pointers refer to that bucket?
questions.explanation: Two low bits identify this bucket, while the directory examines four. The remaining two bit positions can be 00,01,10,11: four directory labels refer to the same bucket. Thus 2^(g−d)=2^(4−2)=4; local depth counts bits, not pointers.

questions.prompt: Using the low bits, with g=3 and h(k)=22 (10110₂), which directory entry is selected?
questions.explanation: The three low bits are 110. The three high bits, 101, are not used.

questions.prompt: What does local depth describe?
options: The required number of overflow pages
The number of shared hash bits used to distinguish this bucket
The height of a B+ tree
The current number of tuples in the bucket
questions.explanation: Local depth counts distinguishing bits, independently of the current entry count.

questions.prompt: Which relationship holds in a consistent extendible hash index?
options: d = g for every bucket at all times
g equals the sum of all bucket depths d
d ≤ g for every bucket
d > g for every bucket
questions.explanation: The directory uses enough bits to address every bucket, so d cannot exceed g. Many buckets can have d smaller than g.

questions.prompt: What is the central idea for handling a full bucket in extendible hashing?
options: Rehash the entire index whenever any bucket fills
Double every data bucket even when only one is full
Double only the directory without redistributing the full bucket
Split the affected bucket instead of rehashing the entire file
questions.explanation: Extendible hashing redistributes only the bucket being split. Doubling the directory does not mean doubling the data.

questions.prompt: A bucket with capacity 2 and suffix 01 contains hash values 1 and 5. Insert 9 and split using 3 bits. What goes into bucket 001?
options: 1 and 9
1 and 5
5 and 9
All three
questions.explanation: 1=001,5=101,9=1001. The low 3 bits of both 1 and 9 are 001.

questions.prompt: What does an ordinary insertion do when the target bucket still has space?
options: Always rehash every bucket
Add the entry to that bucket
Always double the directory
Always create two new buckets
questions.explanation: Without overflow, no split is needed. Doubling the directory for every insertion would be unnecessary.

questions.prompt: After a split, what determines how entries are redistributed?
options: The current tuple count in each bucket rather than hash bits
The entry RID instead of its search-key hash
One additional bit of the hash
Halving the list by insertion order without examining hashes
questions.explanation: The new bit distinguishes the two suffixes. Entry age or transaction identity does not determine the hash partition.

questions.prompt: Why must a lookup compare actual keys even after selecting a bucket with all g bits?
options: Directory pointers are always wrong
Local depth is always 0
Hash indexes store only sorted keys
Different keys can have the same hash suffix
questions.explanation: A g-bit suffix selects candidates. Having a directory does not eliminate collisions.

questions.prompt: With g=3 and d=2, a split produces a new local depth d=3. Must the directory double?
options: No
Yes, because every split increases global depth
Yes, because the new local depth equals global depth
It must double twice so every bucket has one directory pointer
questions.explanation: The new depth does not exceed g, so only pointers change. Not every split requires doubling.

questions.prompt: With g=3 and d=3, a split needs one more bit. How does the directory change?
options: It keeps 8 entries and g remains 3
It grows from 8 to 16 entries
It grows from 3 to 4 entries
It grows from 8 to 9 entries
questions.explanation: Representing depth 4 requires 2^4 entries. Adding just one entry is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Does doubling the directory require copying the data in every bucket?
options: Yes; every bucket must become two buckets
No pointers need to be updated
No; it mainly duplicates pointers and handles the bucket being split
Yes; every tuple is duplicated
questions.explanation: Duplicating pointers is different from duplicating data. Only the split bucket needs redistribution.

questions.prompt: After directory doubling, what happens to the local depth of a bucket that was not split?
options: It must increase by 1
It must decrease by 1
It must equal the new global depth
It remains unchanged
questions.explanation: Increasing global depth does not mean that every bucket needs another distinguishing bit.

questions.prompt: What must be ensured before safely shrinking a directory?
options: Removing a directory bit preserves all necessary distinctions between buckets
It is enough for one bucket to have an empty slot
It is enough for overall occupancy to be below 50%, regardless of local depths
It is enough for the directory to have an even number of entries
questions.explanation: Shrinking is a structural change with specific preconditions. A single deletion is not enough to establish that it is safe.

questions.prompt: How many low bits of a nonnegative integer are used by h(k)=k mod 16?
questions.explanation: Because 16=2^4, the function uses 4 low bits. The modulus itself is not the bit count.

questions.prompt: How are keys 0,16,32,48 distributed by h(k)=k mod 16?
options: Each key must enter a different bucket
All enter bucket 4
All enter bucket 0
They enter buckets 0,1,2,3
questions.explanation: All these keys are divisible by 16, so their low 4 bits are 0. A power-of-two modulus is vulnerable to this pattern.

questions.prompt: What is a suitable goal for a hash function used frequently in a DBMS?
options: Maximise computation cost regardless of collisions
Preserve only numerical order
Avoid collisions for a few sample keys and ignore the rest
Keep computation cheap and distribute the workload well
questions.explanation: Hash lookups need both speed and a good distribution. Preserving order is not the usual goal of hashing.

questions.prompt: Does a prime modulus guarantee no collisions when the key domain is larger than the number of buckets?
options: No
Yes; a prime produces a one-to-one mapping for every domain
Yes, as long as the keys are unique
Yes, as long as the keys are integers
questions.explanation: The pigeonhole principle still applies. Unique keys do not imply unique buckets.

questions.prompt: A hash function distributes distinct keys evenly, but key X occurs in 90% of the tuples. What can still happen?
options: Occurrences of X are naturally spread evenly across buckets
The bucket containing X becomes very large
Every bucket is guaranteed to contain the same number of tuples
Overflow is never needed
questions.explanation: Distributing distinct keys evenly does not remove frequency skew. Equal keys have the same hash.

questions.prompt: A static index has 100 primary buckets, and the table grows 10 × without rebuilding. What is the main risk?
options: Every bucket local depth increases with the row count
The file automatically maintains exactly 20% free space
Overflow chains grow
The directory automatically grows 10×
questions.explanation: A static bucket count does not adapt automatically. Directories and depths belong to a different, dynamic scheme.

questions.prompt: A table shrinks substantially but retains its original primary area. What is the space consequence?
options: Every primary page is immediately returned to the disk manager
Only overflow pages become primary pages
Space utilisation is unaffected
Many lightly used buckets still occupy space
questions.explanation: Static allocation can waste space after shrinkage. It does not automatically compact the entire file.

questions.prompt: Rehashing from 8 to 16 primary buckets may require processing which entries?
options: Entries throughout the index under the new hash mapping
Only the newly inserted entry in every case
Only bucket 0, regardless of the keys
Only the pointer count changes; data placement is ignored
questions.explanation: Changing a static mapping requires redistributing entries, unlike a local split in extendible hashing.

questions.prompt: What concurrency advantage can static buckets provide?
options: Rehashing never affects access
An insertion can limit locking to the affected bucket or page
No concurrent write ever needs locks
Every insertion must lock the entire database
questions.explanation: Static placement can simplify local locking. It does not eliminate the need for concurrency control.

questions.prompt: When comparing periodic rehashing with extendible growth, which trade-off is correct?
options: Static rehashing never reads data
Extendible hashing does not use a directory
Rehashing does broad work in batches; extendible hashing usually splits locally
Both always copy the entire file on every insertion
questions.explanation: The two schemes adapt differently. The local-growth advantage of extendible hashing does not mean every static update processes the entire file.
